edges.rationale: Genesis 2–3 places the tree within the command and transgression narrative.
Genesis 3 narrates expulsion after disobedience.
Genesis 4 narrates Cain killing Abel.
Genesis 4:15 reports a protective sign for Cain.
Genesis 6–9 associates Noah with the flood.
Genesis 6–8 includes animals preserved in the ark.
2 Samuel 11 narrates David’s actions involving Uriah.
Divine forgiveness and accountability require comparison of 2 Samuel 12 and Psalm 51.
Canonical gospel passion narratives describe Jesus’ crucifixion.
Atonement is a theological interpretation of the crucifixion, developed in multiple models.
Christian theological accounts link atonement with reconciliation.
The relation between complete knowledge and future contingents is debated in philosophy of religion.
Divine foreknowledge and free agency form a classic compatibility problem.
Preventing harm may constrain or preserve agency depending on the proposed intervention.
Institutional speech acts depend on conventions and recognized authority.
Framing can change judgments, but effects are conditional and context-dependent.
Misestimated peer attitudes can maintain a publicly perceived norm.
Changes in willingness to reveal private beliefs can produce rapid apparent opinion shifts.
Recommender incentives and attention allocation interact; direction and magnitude require study.
The enchantment sense of spell has a historical linguistic relationship to speech/story traditions.
John 1 uses the Greek Logos within a distinct theological account.
Naming is narratively prominent in Genesis; power implications require textual argument.
